tasks.description: Create a module file `mymath.py` with functions `add(a,b)` and `multiply(a,b)`. Import and use them in your main script.
tasks.hint:
Create `mymath.py` with two function definitions.
In your main script: `import mymath; print(mymath.add(3, 4))`
Or: `from mymath import add, multiply` to use names directly.
tasks.solution:
with open('mymath.py', 'w') as f:
    f.write('def add(a, b):\n')
    f.write('    return a + b\n\n')
    f.write('def multiply(a, b):\n')
    f.write('    return a * b\n')

import mymath
print(mymath.add(3, 4))
print(mymath.multiply(3, 4))

from mymath import add
print(add(10, 20))
tasks.walkthrough:
The first block creates mymath.py in the working folder. In a real project you'd write that file in your editor instead.
`import mymath` loads it, and its functions are reached with a dot. `from mymath import add` brings one name in directly.

tasks.description: Use `if __name__ == '__main__':` in your module. Show that the block only runs when the file is executed directly, not when imported.
tasks.hint:
Python sets `__name__` to `'__main__'` when a file is run directly.
When imported as a module, `__name__` is the module's filename (without .py).
Code under `if __name__ == '__main__':` is like a 'main entry point'.
tasks.solution:
module_code = '''
def greet():
    return "Hello from the module"

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("This only runs when executed directly")
'''

with open('greeter.py', 'w') as f:
    f.write(module_code)

import greeter
print(greeter.greet())
print('Module name when imported:', greeter.__name__)

import subprocess, sys
print(subprocess.run([sys.executable, 'greeter.py'], capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.strip())
tasks.walkthrough:
When `greeter` is imported, its `__name__` is 'greeter', so the guarded print doesn't fire.
The last lines run greeter.py as its own program using subprocess, and this time the guarded print does appear, because `__name__` is '__main__' there.

tasks.description: Create a package folder `utils/` with `__init__.py` and a `strings.py` module inside. Import from the package.
tasks.hint:
Create the folder `utils/`, then inside it create `__init__.py` (can be empty) and `strings.py`.
`from utils.strings import some_function` imports from the package.
`__init__.py` makes the folder a Python package.
tasks.solution:
import os

os.makedirs('utils', exist_ok=True)
with open('utils/__init__.py', 'w') as f:
    f.write('')
with open('utils/strings.py', 'w') as f:
    f.write('def shout(text):\n')
    f.write('    return text.upper() + "!"\n\n')
    f.write('def whisper(text):\n')
    f.write('    return text.lower() + "..."\n')

from utils.strings import shout, whisper
print(shout('hello'))
print(whisper('HELLO'))
tasks.walkthrough:
The folder plus an `__init__.py` file is what makes `utils` a package.
The dotted import path mirrors the folder structure: `utils.strings` is `utils/strings.py`.

tasks.description: Use `dir()` and `help()` to explore the `math` module. Print all available names, then get help on `math.factorial`.
tasks.hint:
`import math; print(dir(math))` lists all names in the module.
`help(math.factorial)` prints the docstring and signature.
This is how you explore any module you're unfamiliar with.
tasks.solution:
import math

names = [name for name in dir(math) if not name.startswith('_')]
print(names)
print()
help(math.factorial)
tasks.walkthrough:
`dir` returns every attribute name in the module. Filtering out the ones starting with an underscore hides internal bits.
`help` prints the docstring and signature, which is the quickest way to learn what a function does.

tasks.description: Use `importlib.reload()` to reload a module after changing its content (simulate hot-reloading).
tasks.hint:
`import importlib; importlib.reload(mymodule)` re-executes the module file.
This is useful for development/testing — changes take effect without restarting Python.
Note: existing references to old objects are not updated.
tasks.solution:
import importlib

with open('settings.py', 'w') as f:
    f.write('DEBUG = False\n')

import settings
print('Before:', settings.DEBUG)

with open('settings.py', 'w') as f:
    f.write('DEBUG = True\n')

print('After edit, before reload:', settings.DEBUG)
importlib.reload(settings)
print('After reload:', settings.DEBUG)
tasks.walkthrough:
The module is imported, then the file on disk is changed. The imported copy still shows the old value because Python cached it.
`importlib.reload` re-executes the file and the new value appears.

lesson.intro:
As a program grows, one file stops being enough. A module is just a `.py`
file you import; a package is a folder of them. Today is about splitting code
across files and understanding what `import` actually does.

This app has a single editor, so the solutions create the extra files with
`open()` before importing them. In a normal project you'd make the files in
your editor and skip that part.

sections.heading: Your own module
sections.body:
Any `.py` file in the same folder can be imported by its name without the
extension. The functions inside become `module.function`.
sections.code:
with open('mymath.py', 'w') as f:
    f.write('def add(a, b):\n    return a + b\n')
    f.write('def multiply(a, b):\n    return a * b\n')

import mymath
print(mymath.add(3, 4))
print(mymath.multiply(3, 4))

sections.heading: if __name__ == '__main__'
sections.body:
When a file is run directly, Python sets `__name__` to `'__main__'`. When
it's imported, `__name__` is the module's name. So code under that `if`
only runs when the file is the program, not when it's a library. It's
where test code or a script's entry point goes.
sections.code:
code = '''
def greet():
    return "hi from greeter"

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("greeter run directly")
'''
with open('greeter.py', 'w') as f:
    f.write(code)

import greeter
print(greeter.greet())
print(greeter.__name__)

sections.heading: Packages: a folder with __init__.py
sections.body:
A folder containing `__init__.py` (which can be empty) is a package.
Modules inside are imported with dots: `from utils.strings import shout`.
sections.code:
import os
os.makedirs('utils', exist_ok=True)
open('utils/__init__.py', 'w').close()
with open('utils/strings.py', 'w') as f:
    f.write('def shout(s):\n    return s.upper() + "!"\n')

from utils.strings import shout
print(shout('hello'))

sections.heading: Exploring a module: dir and help
sections.body:
`dir(module)` lists every name inside. `help(thing)` prints its
documentation. Both are handy when you're in a module you don't know.
sections.code:
import math
names = [n for n in dir(math) if not n.startswith('_')]
print(names[:6])
help(math.factorial)
sections.output:
['acos', 'acosh', 'asin', 'asinh', 'atan', 'atan2']
Help on built-in function factorial in module math:

factorial(n, /)
    Find n!.

sections.heading: reload: pick up changes without restarting
sections.body:
Python imports a module once and caches it. If the file changes,
`importlib.reload(module)` re-runs it. Mostly useful in interactive
sessions.
sections.code:
import importlib

with open('version.py', 'w') as f:
    f.write('VERSION = 1\n')
import version
print(version.VERSION)

with open('version.py', 'w') as f:
    f.write('VERSION = 2\n')
importlib.reload(version)
print(version.VERSION)

watch_out: Naming your file the same as a standard module (`random.py`, `json.py`). Your file shadows the real one.
Importing before the file exists. In these tasks the `open()` that writes the module must come before the `import`.
`import mymath.py` is wrong. Leave off the extension.
`reload` updates the module object, but names you imported with `from module import name` keep the old value.
